reader_question: Have the rules been moving toward voters or away from them?
grade_line: Documented: the atlas’s dated log, coded by the atlas
title: Of the 64 rule changes in its log, the atlas codes 24 as moving the rules toward voters and 24 as moving them away.
measure_line: Each square is one entry in the repair log, the dated list of changes to the rules that decide who officials answer to, kept by the atlas, Oath & Action’s own research, placed by year and by the atlas’s direction code, 1965 to the November 3, 2026 ballot. The count above each year gives every entry the log holds that year.
notes: As of November 11, 2026: voters have cast their ballots on all three measures this chart counts as pending (repair-log entries RL62, RL63 and RL64), and none is certified. Massachusetts Question 3, for one all-candidate primary with the top two advancing, failed 61.0 percent to 39.0 in the unofficial count. Missouri Proposition A, the referendum on the 2025 congressional map, failed 61.8 percent to 38.2 in the unofficial statewide count; a no vote keeps the 2022 districts. Alaska Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal the top-four primary and ranked-choice general elections, trailed 47.4 percent to 52.6 in the unofficial count of November 10, with mailed and overseas ballots still to come. Sources: NBC Boston, Massachusetts ballot question results, November 9, 2026, a secondary source; State of Alaska, Division of Elections, 2026 General Election summary report, unofficial results, November 10, 2026; St. Charles County, Missouri, unofficial statewide returns, November 4, 2026. Retrieved November 11, 2026.
The first year group, To 2012, holds every entry from 1965 to 2012.
Open squares count toward voters and solid squares away from voters; the band below holds entries that went neither way.
The atlas chose which 64 changes to record, and it records more of recent years: 33 of the 64 entries fall in 2025 and 2026.

How the atlas codes direction: Each row is coded by one of five labels. ‘Toward voters’ means the change widens who can register, vote or have a ballot counted, makes each vote weigh more equally, opens the contest that decides the seat, makes political money more limited or more visible, strengthens an independent check on officials, or adds to household security through automatic benefits. ‘Away from voters’ means the change does the reverse. ‘Voters kept existing rules’ means a ballot measure failed and the rules in force stayed, coded the same whichever way the measure would have moved power. ‘Pending’ means voters or courts have not yet decided. ‘Mixed’ means the change moved in both directions at once or left the rules in practice unchanged; the row’s own note says which. Three rules apply across parties. A partisan redraw of district maps in the middle of a decade is coded away from voters whichever party draws it and whether or not voters approved it; a court order that blocks one is coded toward voters, and one that lets it take effect is coded away. A change that widens who takes part in the deciding round (open or all-party primaries) or lets voters rank candidates is coded toward voters, and a law or amendment that bans those options is coded away; readers may weigh these entries differently, and the atlas’s profiles of those two reforms rate confidence in their effect on moderation as low.
A map redrawn in the middle of a decade counts as away from voters whichever party draws it: Texas’s HB 4 (August 2025) and California’s Proposition 50 (November 2025) both count as away.

One entry, RL47, dated March 2026 and drawn as the ringed square marked 19 states, stands for all 19 state bans on ranked-choice voting; Missouri’s and Indiana’s bans also have entries of their own. Eleven of the 19 passed before 2025, and 10 of those have no entry of their own.
A row’s direction describes only the rule’s effect on who officials answer to.
source_line: Source: Oath & Action’s systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, repair log of 64 dated rule changes, August 6, 1965 to the November 3, 2026 ballot, United States: federal, state and local. Snapshot of October 15, 2026. Directions are the atlas’s own codes, set out in its coding note; each row cites its own source. One entry, New York City’s 1988 small-donor matching law, rests on a source the atlas did not check.
alt: A unit chart with one square for each of the 64 entries in the atlas’s repair log, placed by year. The atlas codes 24 entries toward voters, above the year line, and 24 away from voters, below it; 16 went neither way. Most entries fall in 2024 to 2026, and 2026 holds the most moves away from voters.

chart_notes: Rows: all entries per year; toward voters, above the year labels; away from voters, below them; neither way (voters kept existing rules when a ballot measure failed, mixed, or pending on November 3, 2026). Years with no entry keep their column and print 0.
Key: open square, toward voters; solid square, away from voters; gray square, voters kept existing rules; hatched square, mixed; dashed outline, pending on November 3, 2026.

notes_internal: No disclosure (DR-100, D2-1756); Phase 2 printed it under this chart.
X1: the kit now draws Phase 2's mirror, the neither-way band, every year from 2013 with 2019 and 2023 at 0, and the ring around RL47, so the notes describe them again.
W09: Phase 2's 'not every rule change in the country' and 'carries no judgment' are recast without the corrective turn; the facts are unchanged.

Checked by script: 24 toward, 24 away, 10 voters kept existing rules, 3 mixed, 3 pending; three entries to 2012; 33 in 2025 and 2026; 11 of the 19 bans before 2025, of which only Missouri's (RL30) has its own entry.

D3-98: the first note, dated under Rule 13.10, gives the three November 3 outcomes as the record stands, with their sources; the squares keep V7's codes. Statistics P2-S10: the measure line glosses the repair log.
